summary: Describes a URN namespace engineered by the Commission for the Management and Application of Geoscience Information for naming persistent resources. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This gives a group that studies the earth a permanent-name scheme for its data and documents.

questions: what is the geological timescale urn
subtitle: Permanent names for geoscience data, standards, and resources

tldr.problem: Geoscience organizations (geological surveys, research institutions) need to share data and standards using schemas and registries. These resources need persistent, global identifiers.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5138 registers the URN namespace 'cgi' with IANA for the Commission for the Management and Application of Geoscience Information. The namespace structure supports different resource types (schemas, registers, feature types, classifiers) managed through a naming authority (CGINA).
tldr.outcome: Geoscience organizations can now assign formal, globally unique URNs to their standards, data definitions, and resources, enabling interoperability in geospatial systems.

today: RFC 5138 remains the registration of the 'cgi' URN namespace with IANA. It has not been obsoleted and is used by geoscience organizations and standards bodies that work with CGI-endorsed interchange specifications.

sections.title: Geoscience Information and Standards
sections.content:
The Commission for the Management and Application of Geoscience Information (CGI) is part of the International Union of Geological Sciences. Its members are primarily geological surveys and organizations responsible for providing geoscience information to the public. CGI develops standards for exchanging geoscience data across networks, complementing traditional printed maps.

This work requires many resources: XML schemas, data registers, feature definitions, and classifier systems. Geoscience organizations need persistent, location-independent identifiers for these resources so that systems built in different countries can reliably reference the same definitions. RFC 5138 provides this by registering the URN namespace 'cgi' with IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: Geologists work in many countries, and they need to agree on the names and definitions for rock types, geological periods, and geological features. This RFC gives them official Internet names for all their definitions.

sections.title: The CGI URN Namespace Structure
sections.content:
The urn:cgi: namespace has the structure urn:cgi:{CGIResource}:{ResourceSpecificString}. Each URN identifies a specific class of resource (called CGIResource) and then a specific instance within that class.

The CGIResource component names the type of resource: document, register, xmlns (XML namespace), schema, featureType, classifierScheme, classifier, feature, object, or others. The ResourceSpecificString then identifies a specific resource of that type. For example:

  • urn:cgi:document:CGI:CGIIdentifierScheme identifies the document describing the identifier scheme itself
  • urn:cgi:classifier:ICS:StratChart:2004:Silurian identifies the Silurian geological period from the 2004 Stratigraphic Chart
  • urn:cgi:featureType:CGI:GeoSciML:2.0:Fault identifies the Fault feature type in version 2.0 of GeoSciML
sections.plainLanguage: Each CGI URN has two parts: what kind of thing it is (a document, a rock type, a geological period) and which specific thing it is (which document, which rock, which period).

sections.title: Resource Types and Examples
sections.content:
The RFC provides nine detailed examples of CGI URNs. Resources include:

  • Documents and registers: Official specifications and lists of registered items
  • XML namespaces: Formal identifiers for XML schema definitions, such as urn:cgi:xmlns:CGI:GeoSciML:2.0 for version 2.0 of GeoSciML (Geoscience Markup Language)
  • Schemas: Information models and their representations, like urn:cgi:schema:GGIC:MineralOccurences:1.0:XMI
  • Feature types: Geographic and geological feature definitions (faults, mineral deposits, etc.)
  • Classifiers: Controlled vocabularies like the Stratigraphic Chart that names geological periods, or lithology (rock type) classifiers
  • Feature and object instances: Specific geological features or data objects, often using UUIDs as unique identifiers

The CGI Naming Authority (CGINA) manages the registration of new resource classes and assigns identifiers within each class. Other organizations (like the International Commission for Stratigraphy) can be delegated responsibility for portions of the namespace.
sections.plainLanguage: CGI URNs can name many kinds of things: documents that explain standards, lists of registered items, official data definitions, rock types, geological time periods, and even individual geological observations recorded in the field.

sections.title: Persistence and Interoperability
sections.content:
The key value of the CGI URN namespace is persistence. Once a resource is assigned a URN, that binding is permanent, regardless of where the resource moves or whether organizational structures change. This allows systems built years apart in different countries to reliably refer to the same definitions.

The namespace design also enables delegation. CGINA can assign responsibility for sub-sections of the namespace to other organizations (such as the International Commission for Stratigraphy managing geological time periods, or Geoscience Victoria managing lithology classifiers). This allows the system to scale while maintaining uniqueness and persistence.

The design was based on experience from the Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC), another standards body working in related domains. Like OGC, CGI provides a web-based registry and resolver so organizations can look up and access the resources identified by these URNs. There are no special security considerations beyond those normal for URNs in general.
sections.plainLanguage: A URN assigned today will still work in 20 years, even if the geoscience organization moves or changes its website. Different geoscience groups can manage different parts of the naming system while staying coordinated.

references.text: Daigle, L., van Gulik, D., Iannella, R., and P. Faltstrom, "Uniform Resource Names (URN) Namespace Definition Mechanisms", BCP 66, RFC 3406, October 2002.
